# Public Opinion

## Abstract

Lippmann's unpublished notes and drafts alongside key contemporary works, new light is shed on how the book's origins predated the First World War and how its argument went beyond debates about technocratic government. Lippmann's main agenda was to contest liberal-constitutionalist theories of public opinion; his core intervention was to develop a social psychology of opinion formation. He drafted and wrote Public Opinion as a descriptive account of democratic politics under modern conditions. Instead of simply prescribing technocratic solutions, Lippmann framed a starker paradox: democracy through public opinion defined modern politics, but modernity also made opinion formation ever more difficult. Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion was published in 1922 and has shaped much debate over the century since. 1 It remains a classic text in communications studies and a frequent point of reference in US history and political science. Scholars often read Public Opinion as a prescriptive argument for technocratic government: rule by experts. They also see Lippmann's wartime propaganda work as crucial biographical context for the book's composition. Edward Purcell's study of The Crisis of Democratic Theory argued that Lippmann's postwar "disillusionment … combined with his consistent political elitism" to produce Public Opinion's case for expert rule within "a chastened, elite-controlled democracy." 2 Stronger versions of this argument suggest that Lippmann not only theorized but also embraced "the manufacture of consent." 3 Communications scholars have shown how Lippmann's ideas were more nuanced than such accounts claim and more critical of propaganda in

particular. 4 But the book as a whole has not been reconsidered in depth. Public Opinion is still read through old heuristics that frame its major concerns as expert rule and propaganda.

This article explores and reframes Lippmann's writing of Public Opinion. By examining his unpublished papers at Yale University, which contain draft chapters and reading notes, and by relating this archival evidence to wider intellectual and political contexts, the article sheds new light on the book's argument and interlocutors. 5 Public Opinion was primarily about the concept of public opinion in democratic theory, but this fact can be obscured by focusing on his final chapters about expertise. Lippmann's main targets were liberal constitutionalists who theorized public opinion through state institutions. His key intervention was to develop a social psychology of opinion formation in the modern world. Lippmann's book did not just articulate wartime experience or postwar disillusionment, but also developed a prewar agenda that went back to Graham Wallas, his teacher and mentor. By engaging with Wallas, James Bryce, William James, and many others, Lippmann built his conceptual vocabulary of "pseudo-environments" and "stereotypes" to explain how modern citizens formed opinions and shaped political outcomes. 6 His book concluded that better expertise was crucial for government decisions, because citizens were not omnicompetent, but he did not think democracy itself could be governed by a technocratic elite of omniscientomnipotent experts. Public Opinion was drafted and written as a descriptive account of democratic politics under modern conditions.

Beyond his engagements with other theorists, Lippmann's book was deeply embedded in the political world of the United States in the 1920s. While the First World War mattered here, much else mattered too. 7 This article reveals a wider range of contexts for Public Opinion's composition than wartime propaganda alone. Lippmann theorized modern democracy through politicians like Warren Harding, campaigns for women's suffrage, party machines and conventions, and new media technologies like instant photography, motion pictures, and mass-circulation newspapers. What might democracy mean in a complex plural society with an imageobsessed media? How were opinions shaped by the public debates and political institutions that existed? Why had the American people voted for Harding's vision of normalcy in 1920? These were all questions that Lippmann explored as well as war propaganda. While the dynamics of postwar disillusionment shaped the book, Public Opinion was a more general meditation on modernity's social formations and political consequences. 8 Before and after the war, indeed throughout his career, Lippmann claimed to offer disenchanted perspectives on modern democracy. In Public Opinion, he examined the nature and scope of contingent political contests over public opinion's content.

Instead of simply prescribing technocratic solutions, Lippmann's book framed a starker paradox about modern democracy. Public Opinion argued that democracy was the main political reality of the modern world, and that public opinion defined its essence and processes. But the book also claimed that modernity produced serious problems for opinion formation, which could limit or damage political actions and choices. For Lippmann, the difficult task of modern democracy was making progress through politics while negotiating this paradox. He saw democracy's problems as deep political dilemmas for the public itself, not narrow technical issues that experts could resolve. Amid recent anxiety over the prospects for democracy, as well as renewed interest in its principles of uncertainty, historicizing Public Opinion can provide useful perspectives on an influential work of American political thought. 9 he first part of this article will examine the origins of Public Opinion through Lippmann's reading notes and draft chapters. The second part will explore the main categories of his social psychology: pseudo-environments and stereotypes. The third portion will consider Lippmann's attempt to explain opinion formation with these categories. The fourth will evaluate his claims about government, expertise, and democratic paradox.

## Social Psychology and Political Science

Lippmann's conceptual agenda for Public Opinion was broadly in place before the First World War. His thinking had been shaped by Graham Wallas, a British political scientist and Fabian socialist who taught him at Harvard University and became a mentor. 10 Wallas's Human Nature in Politics, published in 1908, was a polemic against institutional political science and a plea for analyzing human beings themselves. Wallas argued that jurists like James Bryce misunderstood politics by prioritizing constitutional analysis, and that psychologists like William James offered resources for a new political science. 11 From Wallas's teaching and writing, Lippmann took the lesson that politics involved psychological complexities as well as constitutional structures and economic conflicts. Wallas framed the modern state itself through social psychology in The Great Society, which he published in 1914 and dedicated to Lippmann.

The idea of "the Great Society" was crucial to Lippmann's intellectual biography. For him and Wallas, it broadly meant the social environment wrought by modernity. The Great Society was about urbanization, industrialization, and mass communication, which produced more pluralistic cultural patterns and specialized divisions of labor. Modern conditions were vast, complex, fractured, and new, "without precedent," Wallas claimed, "in the history of the world." Wallas saw public opinion as a crucial, difficult political variable in the Great Society. He wrote that "the 'public opinion' of a new suburb, where no one knows his neighbour and each season-ticket holder reads his newspaper in silence in the morning train," was very different from "the 'public opinion' of an agricultural village on the day after some event which every householder has discussed with every other." 12 he basic ambition of Lippmann's Public Opinion was to provide a democratic theory for the Great Society by developing Wallas's social psychology. The book was a long-gestating project, which Lippmann pursued amid other priorities, but his early writings outlined its major themes. In 1913, Lippmann's Preface to Politics argued that Wallas and William James "illustrate the changing focus of political thought," because they discussed the intricate psychologies of human political actors. 13 In 1914, Drift and Mastery celebrated Wallas and James, while arguing that "what we grandiloquently call the will of the people" needed rethinking in order for the Great Society to sustain a "democratic purpose." 14 Then in June 1914, on vacation in Maine, Lippmann sketched out some "Notes on Public Opinion" in an unpublished manuscript.

These notes were rough jottings rather than detailed plans but show Lippmann thinking about Public Opinion's main concept before the war broke out in Europe. He wrote that "the ideal of democracy" involved a particular mode of opinion formation: "self-conscious people forming judgments on weight of evidence, and initiating from their own thoughts." But "the reality is very different," Lippmann continued, because the plural nature of "modern conditions" altered the "kind of opinion" that governed. His notes discussed various aspects of opinion formation, including political parties, federalism, muckraking, and the "great advantages of self-consciousness of interest, class, group, sexrealism, empiricism, enlisting of real passions in social affairs, use of specialists and experts." Self-consciousness, he suggested, could strengthen "the real structure of public opinion." 15 efore the war began, then, Lippmann had developed a social-psychological approach to public opinion and linked this with broader theories of modern democratic politics. While the war deeply shaped his political thinking, particularly in foreign policy and international relations, it cannot simply be seen as the origin of Public Opinion. Lippmann's work for the wartime state was enthusiastic but hardly exceptional. Like many contemporaries, he felt committed to the war effort and swept along by great events. He celebrated American intervention, flitted around the War Department, plunged into postwar planning at the Inquiry, and wrote combat propaganda for the Army. 16 Lippmann's propaganda work has long been emphasized by scholars, but his military career was not very successful ("who is 'Captain' Lippmann," asked Wilson, "and who commissioned him to assess our propaganda?"). 17 Lippmann disliked and criticized George Creel's civilian propaganda operation, the Committee on Public Information. 18 Reviewing Creel's book How We Advertised America in 1920, Lippmann argued that "there is probably no good way of conducting government propaganda," and that "a government based on consent" could not "enter upon the business of manufacturing consent" in any "healthy way." 19 The idea that public opinion could be manufactured long predated the war. Ray Stannard Baker argued in 1906 that railroad corporations "manufactured" consent; Balzac claimed in 1840 that "public opinion is manufactured in Paris." 20 or Lippmann's writing of Public Opinion, the First World War provided distractions and interruptions alongside source material and inspiration. 21 In 1919 he described Public Opinion as "a book on which I've been working intermittently for five years." 22 He refocused on it after the peace conference, Red Scare, and Harding's election.
